summary: On Tuesday, Pope Leo XIV underwent successful thoracic surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, with post-operative tests confirming a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma.
Leo disclosed the discovery during his Sunday, October 11, Angelus address in St. Peter's Square, marking rare transparency about the first major health problem of his 17-month papacy.
Surgeons used a video-assisted technique for the 90-minute operation at Gemelli. The Holy See Press Office reported the procedure was successful with no complications.
Vatican officials canceled all public audiences for Leo through October 20 to allow recovery, with the pontiff expected to remain hospitalized for approximately one week.

Oncologists describe Leo's prognosis as 'excellent' due to early detection; however, his planned November 6–17 trip to South America remains uncertain given the logistical demands of over 31,000 kilometers across a dozen flights.

Security personnel discovered the device on September 30 concealed in toilet paper behind a television in a room frequently used for confidential research, product plans, and strategic discussions.
OpenAI used internal AI models to identify Alfozan, while prosecutors allege a chatbot account linked to his spouse researched "build a continuous audio recorder" and queried meeting room locations.
The company terminated Alfozan, who faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted of using a device to intercept oral communications.
FBI Director Kash Patel stated protecting U.S. AI innovation is among the bureau's highest counterintelligence priorities, as federal authorities continue their investigation into the breach.
title: OpenAI Employee Arrested over Hidden Listening Device, Company Says

The bank admitted it "failed to maintain" an anti-money laundering program and neglected to report over $5 billion in suspicious transactions to the Financial Crimes Enforcement Network , with over $1 billion involving national security risks including Chinese Money Laundering Networks.

As part of the settlement, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency levied a $750 million fine—the largest ever by that agency—while the institution settled "its potential civil liability for 475 apparent violations" of sanctions programs targeting Russia, Iran, and Burma.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that compliance failures expose the U.S. financial system to significant illicit finance risks, stating, "Today's actions send a clear message that even the biggest financial institution are not above the law."

Processing $450 trillion in corporate payments and about $4.5 trillion for 70 million individual clients annually, the bank reports third-quarter earnings on Wednesday, facing heightened regulatory scrutiny.
title: Bank of America hit with more than $1.2 billion in penalties over money-laundering violations

Anger stems from allegations that Jane Doe was sexually assaulted by multiple men at Chi Phi two years ago; a rally on Monday drew thousands demanding justice after authorities did not pursue charges in 2024.

Black Students United co-president Kennedy Young demanded trauma-informed training for university police and minimum sanctions for offenders, while Cornell's media relations office did not respond to requests for comment.
In response to backlash, Cornell announced yesterday that former federal prosecutor Sally Yates will lead an independent review of the university's handling of the 2024 case.

U.S. Senator Tim Kaine and U.S. Representative Debbie Dingell introduced two federal bills requiring independent campus advocates and funding for survivor mental health services, counseling, and academic support.
title: Cornell suspends fraternity parties for rest of academic year amid sexual assault controversy

Corruption accusations plagued Guilfoyle in recent weeks, including reports she pressed donor Eric Deters for $100,000 and pushed "governments from Bulgaria to Albania" to sign deals with her foreign associates.

The Journal reported Guilfoyle bragged about "close ties to two Greek tycoons" bankrolling her travel, while the Associated Press noted Trump and Secretary Marco Rubio were "extremely pissed off" debating her termination.

In her resignation announcement, Guilfoyle denied the allegations, stating, "These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity" and citing her decades of public service.

Audio tapes previously captured Guilfoyle urging a Greek businessman to secure her an invite to an Eric Trump dinner, saying she could "deliver the world to you." Trump later told reporters he "didn't like" the reports he had read.
title: White House says US ambassador to Greece Guilfoyle asked to resign

Initially led by tech billionaire Elon Musk, DOGE was tasked with overhauling the government; the administration contends the group acted as a presidential advisory body exempt from the Freedom of Information Act.

The Government Accountability Office reported DOGE overstated its savings, claiming credit for canceled leases predating the group, while Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington continues seeking organizational and financial information.
Critics called the appeal "an obvious delay tactic to keep the American public in the dark about DOGE," highlighting the group's reckless operation amid the upcoming Supreme Court case.
With eight months left on its charter, the Department of Government Efficiency has now been dissolved, and The Supreme Court expects to issue a decision next year.
title: Supreme Court to hear DOGE’s bid to avoid turning over internal documents

Police allege Wang purchased the chemical acrylamide via eBay to poison the tea of a colleague with pending patents; surveillance video allegedly captured her rummaging through the victim's desk.
The victim's wife discovered the chemical while testing the coffee maker used to brew tea, revealing a potential motive tied to intellectual property theft concerns at American universities.
Wang remains jailed without bail in Los Angeles as of Tuesday, with no attorney listed in court documents to represent her in the ongoing case.

Investigators seized laptops and electronic storage devices following her arrest, while reporters attempting to reach Wang via email and LinkedIn have received no response to inquiries about the allegations.
title: A Wyoming Grad Student Who Allegedly Poisoned a Colleague Has Been Arrested Fleeing to China

The competition received a record-breaking 65,403 entries from 121 countries and territories, organized annually by the Natural History Museum, London.
Jury chair Kathy Moran called the photograph "emotionally a gut punch, heartbreakingly poignant," while researchers suggest the behavior may indicate elephants understand or grieve death.
The winning images will be showcased at the Natural History Museum starting Friday, October 16, 2026, running until July 11, 2027, before embarking on a U.K. and international tour.

Museum director Dr. Doug Gurr noted the collection demonstrates the "extraordinary power of wildlife photography ," while British photographer Oscar Whitfield won the Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year title with a dung beetle image.
title: Winning entries for Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026

summary: The family of 23-year-old William Chapman issued a public plea urging people to stop sharing graphic footage of his fatal encounter at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, stating the online circulation is causing severe distress during a period of immense grief.

The appeal followed public backlash against U.S. President Donald Trump , who shared a clip of the attack to his millions of Truth Social followers alongside the caption, "Don't ever mess with nature!".

South Yorkshire Police and local officials reinforced the family's statement, urging the public and media platforms to refrain from sharing or reposting footage out of respect for the victim and the ongoing coronial investigation.

Relatives described Chapman as a bright young man who had struggled with severe mental health issues in recent years, asking the public to allow local authorities to establish the full circumstances surrounding his death.
The City of Doncaster Council opened a formal health and safety investigation into the incident, while park officials confirmed that the Amur tiger involved, named Altai, will not be euthanized.
title: Family of UK tiger attack victim urges end to video sharing after Trump posts footage

summary: On Wednesday, the International Energy Agency warned that global diesel supply constraints will persist well into 2027, driven by prolonged strain and counter-seasonal stock draws ahead of peak winter demand.
Diesel refining margins soared to record highs of almost $95 per barrel in September as attacks linked to the Iran war slashed production and depleted crucial stock cover.

Wholesale diesel prices reached all-time highs of around $220 per barrel in Europe and the United States, with the IEA advising that record prices are "having broad economic consequences by raising the cost of goods and impacting inflation."
Last week, President Donald Trump announced a deal with Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin for Russia to immediately supply 300,000 metric tons of diesel to the global market to offset price rises.

European Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis warned that "now is not a time to ease sanctions on Russia," questioning whether the deal's volumes have macroeconomic significance, while the IEA projects supply shortages will continue through the second half of 2027.
title: Diesel squeeze set to last well into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA says

Federal prosecutors warned they "will have no choice but to seek emergency relief" if officials do not comply, as the November 3 election approaches and Republicans defend narrow majorities in Congress.

Experts note that while states may have added more than 30,000 noncitizens to voter rolls since 2000 due to software glitches and clerical errors, these figures remain too small relative to 170 million registered voters to affect elections.
title: US Justice Department threatens California over alleged noncitizen voters: Reuters

summary: The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled that some nonviolent felony convictions cannot constitutionally trigger the federal ban on gun possession.
The court upheld the restriction against James Bost, whose convictions followed a 2002 carjacking, because his crimes indicated a risk of firearm misuse.
The court ruled that the ban could not apply to Edward Williams based on his earlier driving-under-the-influence convictions.
The rulings followed the Supreme Court ’s 2022 decision requiring modern gun laws to align with the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation.
title: Federal Appeals Court Rules some Nonviolent Felons Can Legally Own Guns

summary: A new Adura-commissioned report claims the UK could lose £10.8 billion in economic value if the government fails to approve the Rosebank oil and Jackdaw gas fields in the North Sea.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has delayed approval since succeeding Sir Keir Starmer in July, prompting Conservative shadow energy secretary Andrew Bowie to urge him to 'finally give the green light' to new North Sea drilling.
Data in the report projects the fields would provide a £4.1 billion tax revenue boost over the next decade and support 9,450 jobs annually, compared to 7,100 if developments do not proceed.

Environmental campaigners, including Oxfam Scotland head Katherine May, oppose the projects, claiming the industry-commissioned report is 'like asking a seagull whether chips should be left unguarded.'

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh stated on Wednesday that any decision must remain 'compatible with our climate commitments' while balancing energy security and the need for affordable power for British households.
title: Rejecting Rosebank and Jackdaw could cost UK economy £10.8bn, study warns

This announcement follows a September agreement between the United States, Denmark, and Greenland that expands the American military presence while reaffirming Danish sovereignty over the territory.

Washington plans to establish two additional military sites at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig to support Trump's proposed "Golden Dome" missile defense system, which he claims will intercept future threats.

While Greenland holds significant rare earth elements and potential oil reserves, experts note that severe Arctic conditions and high extraction costs complicate commercial viability, with no established production on the island.
As diesel averaged $6.2787 a gallon on Wednesday, critics urge the administration to reverse recent deals involving Russia to supply fuel markets, complicating the energy-focused strategy.

summary: On Tuesday, the Axios-Ipsos American Health Index revealed 43% of Americans support government-run health insurance for everyone, compared with 24% opposed and 32% unsure.
A separate KFF survey released last week found 66% of Americans favor Medicare for All, the highest support in a decade amid rising healthcare costs and federal program cuts.

Support remains divided along party lines, with 62% of Democrats and 47% of Independents backing the proposal, while 52% of Republicans oppose it. Top concerns include inferior care quality and high taxpayer costs .

Public trust in political leaders remains low, with only 20% trusting President Trump for health information and 25% trusting Health Secretary Robert Kennedy. Additionally, 49% would avoid candidates accepting pharmaceutical company political action committee money.

Researchers from Yale University found a Medicare for All-type system could save more than 114,000 lives and around $1 trillion annually. Mallory Newall, Ipsos senior vice president for US public affairs, said expanding federal healthcare programs "is a message that can connect with voters.
title: Poll: 43 percent support ‘Medicare for all’

Tehran has sought to exert control over the waterway since the US and Israel launched strikes on February 28, aiming to gain leverage over Washington after US strikes devastated its navy and limited fast-boat operations.

Expanding operations beyond the Strait to the Gulf of Oman, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps began using unarmed spotters in small boats to identify potential targets, according to maritime security sources.

Attacks on commercial vessels have surged to the highest level since the war began, with at least five incidents in the past 48 hours, and the Navy-led Joint Maritime Information Center described the threat as "severe" on Sunday.

Describing the campaign as "a game of chess," one Iranian official warned of complete closure of the Strait, stating that vessels violating restrictions would be safe nowhere, even outside Hormuz waters.
title: Iran shifting tactics to step up attacks on shipping before US vote: Reuters

summary: On Tuesday, Google released Gemini 4 Argon, its new flagship AI model, to Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app and through the Gemini API.
Seeking to reassert itself in the frontier AI race after skipping Gemini 3.5 Pro, Google developed Argon through internal testing with more than 100,000 employees using Antigravity.
Artificial Analysis data shows Argon matches OpenAI 's GPT-6 Astra on the Intelligence Index at 60 percent of the cost, while internal tests showed 35 percent higher AI-generated code production.
Developers can access Argon via the Gemini API at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30, 2026.
After November 30, rates rise to $4 and $20 per million tokens, while Google deploys safety monitors tracking reasoning to block unintended model workarounds.
title: Google launches flagship AI model Gemini 4 Argon for developers, businesses

summary: On Tuesday, the Justice Department announced an international operation that netted 28 arrests and rescued 117 trafficking victims, while Meta removed more than 3.7 million accounts from Facebook and Instagram targeting United States and United Kingdom users.

The crackdown, labeled "Joint Disruption Week," focused on West Africa and involved agencies including the FBI and the National Crime Agency following a new partnership with the United Kingdom, U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro said.

Technology and financial companies including Microsoft, Google, and Binance participated in the operation, sharing more than 30 leads on scam centers and identifying more than $11 million in freezable funds.

Kelly Milliron, acting chief of staff and counselor to the Assistant Attorney General, told reporters the collaboration provides a "consolidated approach" bringing solutions and safety to citizens through joint targeting.

Matthew Floyd, deputy assistant director of the FBI's Criminal Investigative Division, noted that identifying assets is simple, but legally seizing them requires complex investigative work, while some on Capitol Hill question if current anti-scam efforts remain coordinated enough.
title: Global law enforcement agencies, tech firms disrupt West African scam network

summary: On Tuesday, District Judge Timothy Kelly extended an order preventing President Donald Trump's administration from banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico journalists from the White House, maintaining their press access during the legal dispute.
President Trump announced a ban on the three news organizations on September 18, 2026, prompting the outlets to sue and accuse him of unconstitutional retaliation for coverage he dislikes.

Kelly, nominated by Republican President Donald Trump, ruled the outlets are likely to succeed on their constitutional free speech and due process claims, issuing an injunction to preserve the status quo.
The injunction remains in effect until the Court reaches a final judgment, unless an appeals court intervenes, replacing the temporary access granted by the judge last month.

Kelly stated that no one should interpret the decision to suggest that Trump's "concerns about accuracy and fairness in the media " are unfounded, while acknowledging the government's power to protect national security.
title: Judge extends White House access for CNN, MS NOW, Politico amid legal fight

summary: On Tuesday, President Donald Trump announced at a Wasilla, Alaska rally that Taiwan agreed to purchase 30% of output from the Alaska LNG project for 20 years and invest $4.4 billion in development.
This commitment builds on a March 2025 letter of intent signed by CPC Corporation, as Taiwan seeks to secure energy supplies for the island's semiconductor industry amid surging demand.
Taiwan's Ministry of Economic Affairs has not confirmed the specific terms announced by Trump, clarifying that final investment arrangements and binding contracts remain under active negotiation.
The initiative aims to reduce Taiwan's trade surplus with the United States while diversifying natural gas supplies, critical as the island imports more than 90% of its energy.
Developer Glenfarne aims to deliver the project's first gas in 2029, though the pipeline requires additional binding agreements and financing to proceed with construction.
title: Taiwan agrees to buy 30% of gas from Alaska LNG project, Trump says

summary: On Tuesday, Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if reelected next month, explicitly stating he had "zero interest in running for president."

The Atlanta Press Club Loudermilk-Young Debate Series hosted the second and final debate between Ossoff and Republican Rep. Mike Collins, where both candidates traded personal and political attacks ahead of the midterm elections.
Ossoff criticized Collins for alleged ties to Nazi ideology and delaying Epstein file releases, while Collins questioned Ossoff on donor Reid Hoffman and his stance on the 2020 election.
Decision Desk polling averages show Ossoff leading Collins by nearly 10 percentage points as early voting begins in Georgia, crucial for Senate control.

Senate control remains the broader focus for both parties, with Democrats aiming to maintain their majority while national observers continue speculating on Ossoff's potential as a future party standard-bearer.
title: Ossoff Commits to 6-Year Senate Term Amid 2028 Speculation

summary: On Tuesday, the 193-member United Nations General Assembly elected 15 new members to the 47-nation Human Rights Council in an uncontested vote, as all regional groups put forward exactly the number of candidates for available seats.
Human Rights Watch director Louis Charbonneau criticized the process, calling it a "mockery of the word 'election'" and arguing no country should have a seat "handed to them on a silver platter."

Critics highlighted concerns regarding new members, citing "abusive human rights conditions" in Burundi and noting Brazil must "investigate and curb police abuse" following last year's killing of more than 6,500 people by law enforcement.
U.N. spokesman Stephane Dujarric stated that elected members have an added responsibility to protect human rights globally, though the election process remains a matter for the 193 member nations.

Created in 2006 to replace a discredited commission, the council reviews global rights records; President Donald Trump previously withdrew the United States from the council, citing alleged anti-Israel bias.
title: Human rights groups criticize uncontested election of 15 countries to top UN human rights body

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the proposal as “help” for “struggling” universities within a “growing financial crisis,” while foregrounding presidents, students, and employees who “condemned” shifting millions from two-year colleges and demanding longer-term fixes.

Right-Leaning coverage narrows the story to an administrative “reallocation” supporting “financially unstable” universities and the pending vote, de-emphasizing institutional opposition and broader systemic warnings—language that can invite skepticism about taking resources from one group to aid another.
Center coverage bridges both, describing a $31.5 million deficit and “stopgap” remedy, while noting a decade-old warning.
All emphasize the transfer, vote, and 270,000-student system, reflecting tensions over redistribution, institutional survival, and fiscal responsibility.
summary: On Wednesday, the Minnesota State Board of Trustees will vote on a proposal to reallocate up to $25 million annually from two-year colleges to financially struggling universities over four years.

System officials described the proposal as a "stopgap" to address a $31.5 million systemwide deficit that, if left unaddressed, is projected to more than triple by summer 2028 across 26 colleges and seven universities.

If approved, the system would distribute $10 million to St. Cloud State University and $4.8 million to Bemidji State University, while two-year colleges would contribute about three times as much money as four-year universities.

Rose Sargent, treasurer for the student organization LeadMN, called the proposal a "temporary funding bandage" in June, arguing that reallocating resources away from colleges will not solve underlying financial challenges.

Bill Maki, the system's vice chancellor for facilities and finance, acknowledged the plan is "somewhat unprecedented," as officials continue weighing campus closures and mergers to address broader budgetary pressures.
title: Minnesota State weighs plan to transfer money from two-year colleges to help struggling universities

summary: On Tuesday, The Supreme Court declined to hear an appeal by attorney Andrew Parker, leaving intact $122,000 in sanctions against him and his Minneapolis-based firm, Parker Daniels Kibort.

District Judge John Tuchi imposed the penalty after finding the 2022 Arizona voting-machine lawsuit brought for Kari Lake and Mark Finchem relied on "false, misleading, and unsupported factual assertions."

In his petition, Parker argued that sanctions could "chill lawyers' ability to assert unpopular or difficult claims," warning they deter attorneys from bringing "creative, aggressive or novel claims."

The San Francisco-based Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the sanctions in March 2025, while separately overturning related penalties against retired Harvard Law professor Alan Dershowitz due to his limited role.
This final denial concludes a legal battle dating back to the 2022 midterms, cementing the penalty after The Supreme Court previously declined to take up the underlying case in April 2024.
title: Supreme Court turns away Kari Lake lawyer’s challenge to sanctions in Arizona voting machine lawsuit

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames GLP-1s as “blockbuster drugs” that might slow aging and extend life, emphasizing expansive benefits beyond weight loss; right-leaning coverage sharpens that optimism with “reverse biologic aging” and a reported two-to-three-year difference, portraying the drugs as a possible “true longevity treatment.” Center coverage moderates both, stressing researchers are “still figuring out” side effects, industry-linked evidence, and the gap between biological-age measures and actual lifespan.
The pivotal divide is whether preliminary measurements justify a longevity narrative or warrant caution.

All perspectives acknowledge GLP-1s’ roles in diabetes and obesity treatment and their possible aging effects, reflecting broader tensions between innovation-driven optimism and risk-conscious skepticism.
summary: At the 13th annual Aging Research & Drug Discovery conference in Boston, Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk announced data suggesting their GLP-1 drugs, tirzepatide and semaglutide, can reduce biological age by two to three years.

Widely used for obesity and diabetes, GLP-1s have gained popularity, with 11% of Americans now taking them compared to 3% in 2024, prompting scientists to investigate whether they target underlying aging processes.

Research at the University of California at Berkeley showed semaglutide-treated mice lived an average of 834 days, compared to 742 days for placebos, while human data indicated a four-year reduction in heart-related biological age.

Dr. James Kirkland of Cedars-Sinai Medical Center cautioned that these metrics are still in development and not informative for individuals, noting trials only included participants who were already overweight and diabetic.

Scientists continue to study side effects like hair and nail disorders; one recent study reported 66% of GLP-1 users experienced at least one nail issue, as researchers hope to follow participants longer.
title: GLP-1 Drugs Show Potential Anti-Aging Benefits, but More Research Is Needed

summary: On Tuesday, Sotheby unveiled the rare Nanotyrannus fossil nicknamed 'Jodi' at its Manhattan headquarters, where it remains on public view ahead of its October 27 auction.

Research recently confirmed Nanotyrannus as a distinct genus coexisting with Tyrannosaurus rex some 67 million years ago, featuring slender, bladelike teeth and longer forelimbs unlike the 'King of the Tyrant Lizards.'

Montana rancher Jodi Pierson discovered the fossil in 2019, an excavation featured on the Discovery Channel series 'Dino Hunters,' and Sotheby bills it as the 'finest and most complete' Nanotyrannus available, nearly 70% complete with roughly 35 teeth.
The Society of Vertebrate Paleontology opposes private fossil sales, with president Stuart Sumida arguing that no peer-reviewed scientific study can be published on specimens held in private hands.

Sotheby vice chair Cassandra Hatton defended private diggers as 'crucial in the preservation of science' due to university funding shortages, while critics warn that private sales prevent future access for researchers and the public.
title: Rare fossil of T. rex cousin goes on display in New York before heading to auction

Right-Leaning coverage instead emphasizes “animal-loving New Yorkers,” “grueling conditions,” and “extreme heat and cold,” portraying the ban through horse-welfare concerns while personalizing responsibility around Mamdani and de-emphasizing the October 22 vote, 2028 timeline, and Menin’s role.

summary: New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin and Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced Tuesday the Council will vote October 22 on legislation to ban the horse carriage industry, with the ban taking effect June 1, 2028.
Known as Romanch's Law, the bill was renamed following the June death of 18-year-old tourist Romanch Mahajan, who was killed after falling from a runaway horse in Central Park.

The legislation requires the Administration to create a workforce transition program, offering career counseling and financial compensation to drivers, though Transport Workers Union Local 100 has opposed the ban.

With 29 listed sponsors, the bill is expected to pass through the City Council as City Hall spokesperson Sneha Choudhary stated the city worked with stakeholders to "deliver a just transition that protects workers."

For more than 160 years, carriages have operated in Central Park, but officials cite public safety liabilities in the busy area, and the bill would end license renewals while allowing temporary exceptions.
title: Mamdani and City Council Speaker Julie Menin strike deal to ban NYC horse carriage industry

summary: On Monday, Department of Homeland Security agents searched the Washington home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , D-Minn., removing boxes of documents as part of a federal immigration investigation.

Federal investigators have spent recent months scrutinizing the family's immigration history, specifically whether her late father, Nur Omar Mohamed, omitted information on citizenship forms, building on a decade-long inquiry that has not resulted in charges.

Prosecutors issued subpoenas to family members, including one to her sister, Sahra Noor, to gather evidence regarding possible crimes. Grand jury subpoenas do not imply recipients are themselves under investigation.

Norman L. Eisen, a lawyer who has sued the Trump administration, announced Tuesday that a nonprofit group requested a Hatch Act investigation into whether officials "orchestrated" the search, asserting officials "can't use criminal power to affect an election."

Trump singled out Omar at a rally Saturday, two days before the search, while Vice President JD Vance said Tuesday he lacked advance knowledge, stating, "If there's a real case there, we're going to follow the facts.
title: Justice Department Subpoenas Relatives of Representative Omar

summary: This month, Suncor announced a 'definitive agreement' to sell its offshore oil assets in Newfoundland and Labrador to UK-headquartered Ithaca Energy for CAD $1.2 billion, including stakes in Terra Nova, White Rose, and West White Rose projects.

Ithaca is majority-owned by the Israeli Delek Group, which appears on a United Nations database for 'activities that raised particular human rights concerns' in the occupied Palestinian territories and is accused of providing services supporting illegal settlements.

Citing Prime Minister Mark Carney's September 8 commitment to ban trade with illegal settlements, NDP Foreign Affairs Critic Heather McPherson argues the government should stop this acquisition, claiming it contradicts that pledge.

International investors have previously distanced themselves from Delek; Norway's KLP pension fund and sovereign wealth fund divested from the company in recent years, while a similar controversy is unfolding in the United Kingdom regarding Ithaca's stake in the Rosebank oil field.

Energy Minister Lloyd Parrott did not answer questions regarding the takeover, while Global Affairs Minister Anita Anand did not respond to requests for comment, leaving critics to question whether the trade ban includes services and investments beyond goods.
title: Ithaca to Buy Suncor N.L. Assets for $1.2B; Critics Cite UN-Listed Delek Link

summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu discussed potential military strikes against Iran with President Donald Trump last week, seeking action before Israel's October 27 elections, according to reports.
Netanyahu cited alleged Iranian efforts to rebuild nuclear capacity as justification for the proposed strikes during several conversations with Trump over the past two weeks.

President Donald Trump reportedly told Netanyahu to "go ahead and get ready," though officials noted no definitive commitment, while the Pentagon instructed U.S. Central Command to finalize preparations.
Despite initial interest, Trump has reportedly cooled on the proposal, with most advisors recommending continued economic pressure instead of military action.
On Friday, the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps warned it would escalate hostilities, vowing that "its punishment will be definitive" regarding regional shipping routes.

summary: On Tuesday, Illinois Representative Delia Ramirez introduced the "Reimagining Safety Act," legislation that would abolish the Department of Homeland Security and replace it with a "Department of Community Safety" focused on public health-based approaches.

Ramirez cited systemic issues within the department, stating DHS has "always been empowered to violate our rights," following reports of at least 57 deaths in immigration detention and eight street killings by agents during President Donald Trump's second term.
Under the proposal, FEMA and the TSA would move to other departments while the Treasury manages customs duties; the bill would shutter ICE entirely and release detained immigrants within six months.

A DHS spokesperson criticized the proposal Tuesday, claiming such rhetoric contributes to a "more than 1,300% increase in assaults" against agents as the legislation arrives three weeks before an election where immigration remains central.

Former senior DHS official Adam Klein told Newsweek that immigration enforcement practices "deserve serious scrutiny," though he questioned the distance between the proposed legislation and essential operational responsibilities that remain necessary.
title: House Democrat Introduces Bill Seeking to Cut ICE, CBP, Replace DHS

summary: On Tuesday, former United States President Barack Obama received an honorary doctorate from Queen's University Belfast. Queen's President and Vice-Chancellor Professor Sir Ian Greer presented the award, citing Obama's commitment to peace, dialogue, and public service.

The visit marks Obama's first return to Belfast since 2013, when he addressed young people at Waterfront Hall. During Tuesday's ceremony, he reflected on Northern Ireland's progress since the 1998 Good Friday Agreement, calling it a "shining example" of choosing peace.

First-Year Law with Politics student Emma McAllister presented the doctorate, noting Obama's inspiration for youth. The former president praised R-CITY initiatives in Ardoyne and Shankill, stating "that's what peace makes possible."

Following the ceremony, Obama addressed a packed O2 Arena in a conversation hosted by journalist Susan McKay. He urged the crowd to "insist that we can do better than we're doing right now" amid global challenges.

Addressing global instability, Obama admitted he is "not as hopeful as I want to be in the short term" regarding Gaza. He emphasized the need for an "impulse towards kindness" to counter tribal divides.
title: Obama Receives Honorary Doctorate at Queen's University Belfast
